name: Aisha Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly lectures on Monday and Tuesday, contract law and a politics module I actually like. I live in a flat share on Harlow Road with two second years, and we split the cooking badly. Saturday and Sunday mornings I'm behind the counter at a bakery, up at 5:30. My dad drives buses and my mum does home care, so I'm the first one in the family at university, and I feel that every time I open a reading list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I told you so. Half my course is panicking about robot lawyers and I'm sitting there with my paper notebooks. If it's hype, my essays stay mine and the bakery still needs me on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but not calm, because the money worry stays. The room is 420 a month and my parents cover 200 of it. I'll still leave with about 30,000 in debt, hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep the bakery shifts, keep writing my own notes, and join the law society to meet second years who know which firms hire. I'd try to put away 40 a month for summer, when the family help drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit lighter, honestly. But there's a low hum about debt. Last week I stayed up working out what repayments start to bite, and it didn't feel like hype at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the debt hum doesn't go away. What's the first thing you'd cut if the bakery cut your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going out first, then the train home. I only go home once a month anyway. I'd skip my friend Freya's birthday weekend before I'd ask Mum for more, because she already does extra night visits for her clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry that never using AI tools could hold you back, even in this quiet picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, when classmates say it saves them hours. But my tutor said first-year essays are marked on your own thinking. With my essays, I'd rather be slow and mine than quick and flagged by the software.

say: I'd say the **hype** was always louder than the product.
I'd tell friends my **own notes** still beat any chatbot summary.
think: I feel **relieved**, but my **debt** and rent worry is unchanged.
Nothing about **tuition fees** gets cheaper just because AI flopped.
do: **Keep** the weekend bakery shifts and the 5:30 starts.
**Join** the law society to meet second years who know the firms.
**Save** 40 a month for the summer when family help drops.
feel: **Lighter** about the robot-lawyer panic, but still **tense** about money.
S0.quote: With my essays, I'd rather be slow and mine than quick and flagged by the software.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** to AI is a matter of pride and fairness, not fear.
Money is the real pressure; AI is background noise in this world.
Gets her information from tutors and family rather than online.

steps.text: Keep working Saturday and Sunday shifts at the bakery
Put 40 a month into a summer savings pot
Ask the law society for second-year advice on firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this is exactly why we need rules. If AI takes writing and checking, that's paralegal work, and that's the door people like me use to get into law. Somebody has to be told they can't just stop hiring juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me. Everything law firms ask first years to do is reading, checking and drafting. My dad's union fought hard for bus drivers, and I don't see who fights for the junior who never gets hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay out of the chatbots, which my mates think is mad, but I'd go to every talk by the careers service. I'd ask my politics tutor about housing and employment law, because tenants and workers will always need a person. I'd also tell my dad to bring me along to a union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest. Like standing in a queue and watching the front of it get shorter. I'm not panicking, because three years is something, but I'm already counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use the tools, but you say the work they do is what firms hire for. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, to be honest. I know it's a contradiction. If I'm not using the tools I can't judge them, but I also can't unlearn what they do to a first year's job. Maybe I'll learn one in second year, so I can argue against it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if the junior jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firms, and the people who own the software and keep the profit. Not the students using it, even though my friends think I'm being hard on them. If the work moves to software, the gain should be shared, with a tax or a rule.

say: I'd say this needs **regulation** before junior jobs vanish.
I'd argue firms should keep **training** juniors, not skip them.
think: Entry-level **law work** is exactly what software takes first.
I'm afraid nobody speaks up for the **junior** who never gets hired.
do: **Attend** every careers service talk on legal jobs.
**Ask** my politics tutor about housing and employment law.
**Go** with my dad to a union meeting.
feel: **Tight** in the chest, like a shrinking queue.
**Alert** more than panicked, because three years is something.
S1.quote: If I'm not using the tools I can't judge them, but I also can't unlearn what they do to a first year's job.
fieldNote: Notices her own **contradiction** about not using AI and let it stand.
Blames **firms and owners**, not students, in line with her union upbringing.
Anxious because the entry rung of her chosen path is the exposed part.

steps.text: Go to a union meeting with my dad this term
Ask my politics tutor which law areas need people
Write to my local MP about junior jobs
Hold off on specialising until second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go quiet, then get angry online. Two years means I'm in the middle of second year when it lands. I'd say governments are asleep and somebody must stop firms from just switching people off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my degree might not be worth it. By the time I finish I'd be the same age as the new AGI. My parents are paying for a path that may be closed before I walk down it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd phone my dad that night and ask what the union plans. I'd keep the bakery job, because it's cash, and a person still does the baking until 2031. I'd also ask the uni whether I could switch to something like social care or housing policy that people still do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, mostly. Like the floor tilted. I'd lie awake doing sums on my loan and wondering if mum's job is safe too, because carers get talked about as robot work next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your mum's job might be next. Which of those two worries is bigger, your degree or her work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hers. If I have no job I'm one person with a loan. If Mum's hours go, my parents' help stops and Dad can't cover me and the house. I'd take a night shift before I'd let my mum stop working, because her hours are what keep my parents' help coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your friends, who do use AI every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't be so smug. You've been using the thing that replaces you. But I wouldn't push it, they're frightened too, and we'd end up sat in the flat on Harlow Road with a takeaway, arguing and not solving anything.

say: I'd say **governments** are asleep and must protect workers now.
I'd tell my friends **not to be smug** about the tools.
think: My **degree** may be closed off before I finish it.
I'm afraid my mum's **care work** gets targeted after the desk jobs.
do: **Phone** my dad that night to ask the union's plan.
**Keep** the bakery job because it's cash and hands-on.
**Ask** the uni about switching to social care or housing policy.
feel: **Guilty** that my parents are paying for a closing path.
S2.quote: I'd take a night shift before I'd let my mum stop working, because her hours are what keep my parents' help coming.
fieldNote: Her worry **shifts** from her own career to her **mother's** care job.
Anger is aimed at **governments** for not preparing, not at the technology itself.
Said she would take extra shifts; family obligation comes before study.

steps.text: Phone Dad that night and ask the union's plan
Keep the bakery shifts for cash through 2028
Ask the university about switching to social policy
Ask my parents what savings they can still spare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so use them. Governments need to be forced to plan, and I'd want my course to change what it teaches. I'd put it on the student union's agenda.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is exactly one degree plus a bit. I'd graduate into it. So I'm torn between finishing and doing something that's still wanted in 2031. Some days I think it's pointless, other days I think I should become a person who writes the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in law but steer to employment or housing, where people need advocates. I'd join the student union and maybe stand for a rep role. I'd keep the bakery shifts and apply for a summer job at the council, because a public body might hire a human longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. A bit of fire, because five years gives me time to be useful. But also a weight, like I'm being asked to fix the future with a first-year's timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd consider standing as a student rep. What would you actually say to the other students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're the first year group who'll graduate into this, so we shouldn't wait to be handed a plan. We should ask the department what jobs its graduates in 2031 will actually do, and demand honest numbers, not brochures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what do you say to yourself on a bad night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm 18 and I've still got time, and Dad started his job at 40 after the factory shut. We've been through a closing industry before, and my family didn't fall apart. I hold on to that.

say: I'd say students must **demand** honest job numbers from the department.
I'd put it on the **student union's** agenda.
think: Five years means I **graduate** straight into it.
I'm torn between **finishing** law and choosing something still wanted in 2031.
do: **Steer** my modules towards employment and housing law.
**Stand** for a student rep role next autumn.
**Apply** for a summer job at the council.
feel: A bit of **fire**, because five years lets me be useful.
A **weight** of trying to fix the future from a first-year timetable.
S3.quote: We're the first year group who'll graduate into this, so we shouldn't wait to be handed a plan.
fieldNote: Finds **purpose** in organising, which steadies her more than the fear.
Draws strength from her father's late career change after a factory closed.
Still a **law student** at heart: thinks in terms of rules and advocates.

steps.text: Stand for student rep and press the department for numbers
Choose employment and housing law modules
Apply for a summer admin job at the council

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade, so don't treat it as a crisis, treat it as a project. Unions and politicians should be negotiating now about training and sharing the gains. I'd say we have no excuse for being caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels like safety and also like a trap. I'd have time to qualify and work in my thirties. But a decade is long enough for everybody to forget and do nothing, and then it lands in 2036 on the same people who were warned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, aim for a training contract, and pay off as much debt as I can. I'd volunteer at a tenants' advice centre on weekends instead of the bakery once the money allows. I might finally try one AI tool, just to know what I'm arguing about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others. It's like a long winter forecast. You can buy the coat. I'd still feel a bit sick when I think about Mum's home-care job, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might finally try an AI tool. What would make you do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a lecturer showed me the actual limits, a case where it got the law wrong. I don't trust it blindly, but ten years is long enough to be left behind if I'm stubborn, so I'd start with one small task, like checking a reference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about money in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. With ten years I could clear most of the debt before it hits, and maybe help my parents with a deposit on their rented house. In the fast pictures I'd just be surviving. Here I can plan to be generous.

say: I'd say a decade means a **project**, not a crisis.
I'd urge unions to bargain on **training** now.
think: Ten years feels like **safety** and also like a trap.
People may **forget** and do nothing until 2036.
do: **Finish** the degree and aim for a training contract.
**Volunteer** at a tenants' advice centre at weekends.
**Try** one AI tool to check a legal reference.
feel: **Calmer**, like a long winter forecast where you can buy the coat.
Still **uneasy** about my mum's care job.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to be left behind if I'm stubborn, so I'd start with one small task, like checking a reference.
fieldNote: A decade lets her **soften** her anti-AI stance on her own terms.
Money plans turn **generous**: helping her parents becomes thinkable.
Her calm is relative; her mother's job is still the sore point.

steps.text: Volunteer at the tenants' advice centre on Saturdays
Pay 100 a month towards my student debt
Try one AI tool to check a case reference
Finish the law degree and apply for training contracts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. I'd be halfway through the degree with the loan already taken and no time to change. What would help is a clear promise from government that people who can't be placed get paid retraining, and that the gains get taxed. Also firms being told they can't just stop hiring juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: My dad's union fought for bus drivers, and I don't yet see who fights for the junior who never gets hired. Also, people say I'm stubborn about AI like it's a character flaw. It isn't. I just think somebody should be asking who benefits, and I'd rather ask that from outside the room than be quietly absorbed into it.

headlineQuote: My dad's union fought for bus drivers, and I don't yet see who fights for the junior who never gets hired.
portrait: Aisha is an **18-year-old** law student from a family of a bus driver and a home carer, first at university.
She **refuses** AI tools out of fairness and pride, though she admits the contradiction when pushed.
Her instinct is **collective**: unions, regulation and taxing the gains, rather than quietly adapting.
Her **money worry** is constant: about 30,000 in debt and rent partly paid by her parents.
Across scenarios she moves from relief in the quiet world to alarm at 2028, then to steadier planning with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, with a loan taken and no time to change course.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining** and a tax on the gains, so ordinary families share them.
A rule that firms keep **hiring and training** junior staff.
